title: Saved by Mercy, Devoted to Good
summary: Paul grounds gracious public conduct in God’s saving kindness, rebukes profitless disputes, and closes with travel plans and greetings.
historicalContext: Crete had been a Roman province for little more than a century when Paul wrote, and its towns carried a reputation for faction, quarrelling harbors, and impatience with outside rule. Small house churches lived among neighbors who watched them closely and officials who could easily suspect any new religious movement of disorder. Within the congregations, teachers attracted to Jewish legends, genealogies, and disputes over the law were unsettling households and drawing attention away from practical godliness. Titus had been left to set the churches in order, and Paul now gives him a final word for the whole community: live peaceably in public, remember the mercy that rescued you, refuse endless controversy, and deal firmly but patiently with those who divide the flock. The closing lines show a network of traveling workers—Artemas, Tychicus, Zenas, and Apollos—moving through the Mediterranean while Paul plans to winter at Nicopolis.
literaryContext: Chapter 3 completes the movement begun in chapter 2. There Paul addressed household relationships and then supported them with a sweeping statement of grace (2:11–14). Here he widens the view to the church’s conduct toward rulers and outsiders (3:1–2), then again supports the exhortation with doctrine (3:3–7), a single Greek sentence that traces salvation from God’s kindness to the believer’s inheritance. A “faithful saying” formula (3:8) seals that summary and turns it into a charge to stress good works. The warning against foolish questions and the handling of a factious person (3:9–11) echo the false teaching confronted in 1:10–16, framing the letter’s body. Personal instructions and greetings (3:12–15) close the letter in Paul’s customary manner, with a final reminder that good works must meet real needs.
themes: Peaceable, courteous conduct toward rulers and neighbors
Remembering what grace rescued us from
Salvation by mercy through the Spirit’s new birth
Justification, inheritance, and the hope of eternal life
Good works that meet real needs

outline.title: Gracious Citizens in a Watching World
outline.summary: Titus is to remind believers to submit to civil authority, stand ready for every good work, and show gentleness toward all people.

outline.title: The Kindness That Saved Us
outline.summary: Recalling their former bondage, believers learn that God saved them by mercy through the washing of regeneration and the Spirit’s renewal, making them justified heirs of eternal life.

outline.title: Good Works Instead of Empty Quarrels
outline.summary: Titus must insist on the saving message so believers devote themselves to good works, avoid profitless disputes, and admonish and then refuse a factious person.

outline.title: Fellow Workers, Hospitality, and Grace
outline.summary: Paul arranges Titus’s replacement and journey, asks for generous help for traveling workers, and closes with greetings and a benediction for all.

verses.bibleText: Put them in mind to be subject to principalities and powers, to obey magistrates, to be ready to every good work,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Put them in mind” signals that Titus is not introducing novel ethics. The Cretan believers had already been taught these duties, yet every congregation needs regular reminders, especially when new converts arrive with old habits. Having addressed relationships within the household and the church in chapter 2, Paul now turns outward to the believer’s life under civil government and among unbelieving neighbors.

“Principalities and powers” here refers to human rulers and officials at every level, from local magistrates to the imperial administration. Crete had been brought under Roman control about a century before, and its people had a long history of faction and resentment toward outside authority. A movement that worshiped a crucified Jew and spoke of another King could easily be suspected of sedition. Paul therefore asks believers to be “subject” and to “obey magistrates,” the second verb stressing ready compliance with lawful regulations. The instruction carries weight because Paul himself had been beaten, imprisoned, and misjudged by officials; his counsel flows from conviction, not from comfortable experience.

The phrase “to be ready to every good work” widens obedience into active usefulness. Christians are not to be grudging subjects who merely avoid trouble. They should be the first to support what promotes justice, relief, and the common good. The same phrase also marks a boundary. Readiness is for good works. When a ruler commands what God forbids, the believer’s higher loyalty stands, as the apostles declared before the council in Jerusalem. Submission is the rule; disobedience is reserved for the narrow case in which obedience would mean sin.

Behind the whole verse lies the concern that runs through the letter: the conduct of believers either adorns or discredits “the doctrine of God our Saviour” (2:10). Peaceable, cooperative citizens commend the gospel to a suspicious world, and they leave accusers with nothing true to say against the name of Christ.

wordNotes.term: ὑπομίμνῃσκε (hypomimnēske) — put them in mind
wordNotes.explanation: A present imperative meaning “keep reminding.” The form suggests an ongoing pastoral habit rather than a single announcement. Apostolic teaching often works by recalling what believers already know so that familiar truth governs present conduct.

wordNotes.term: ἀρχαῖς ἐξουσίαις ὑποτάσσεσθαι (archais exousiais hypotassesthai) — to be subject to principalities and powers
wordNotes.explanation: Elsewhere Paul can use this pair of nouns for spiritual powers, but the following reference to magistrates shows that civil authorities are meant here. The verb describes accepting one’s place under an ordered authority, the same verb used for the household relationships of chapter 2.

verses.bibleText: To speak evil of no man, to be no brawlers, but gentle, shewing all meekness unto all men.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul moves from public duty to public speech and temper. “To speak evil of no man” translates a verb that can mean to blaspheme; applied to people it means slander, abusive talk, or contemptuous railing. Cretan believers may have been tempted to speak bitterly of corrupt officials or hostile neighbors. Paul allows no exception. Even the unjust are not to be reviled. Truthful criticism of wrongdoing is one thing; the habit of mocking and disparaging those in power, or those of another nation or class, is another, and it corrodes the speaker as surely as it insults the hearer.

“No brawlers” describes people who refuse to fight, the same quality required of an overseer in 1 Timothy 3:3. Crete’s busy ports brought together sailors, traders, and travelers from many nations, and quarrels came easily. In that setting a peaceable Christian stood out. Paul adds the positive side: believers are to be “gentle,” yielding and reasonable instead of insisting on every right, and to show “all meekness unto all men.” The doubled “all” leaves no room for selective courtesy that is warm toward fellow believers and cold toward outsiders.

These qualities are not natural to fallen people, which is why the next verse turns to what believers once were. They are, however, the character of Christ, whose meekness and gentleness Paul invoked when appealing to the Corinthians. A church that speaks well of those who mistreat it, declines to retaliate, and treats every person with considerate respect gives the clearest evidence that the gospel has changed it.

wordNotes.term: ἐπιεικεῖς (epieikeis) — gentle
wordNotes.explanation: The word describes a reasonable, forbearing disposition that does not press its own rights to the limit. It is the opposite of harsh insistence. It appears among the qualities of wisdom from above and of a church leader.

wordNotes.term: πραΰτητα (praytēta) — meekness
wordNotes.explanation: Meekness is strength under the control of God, shown in considerate courtesy and freedom from self-assertion. It is not weakness or timidity. Jesus described himself as meek, and Paul lists meekness as fruit of the Spirit.

verses.bibleText: For we ourselves also were sometimes foolish, disobedient, deceived, serving divers lusts and pleasures, living in malice and envy, hateful, and hating one another.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“For” gives the reason for the gentleness just required. Believers must treat outsiders kindly because they themselves were once no different. Paul includes himself—“we ourselves also”—and the word “sometimes” means “at one time” or “formerly.” The verse is a portrait of life without God, and its purpose is to remove any trace of superiority from the church’s attitude toward the world.

The portrait moves in a descending line. “Foolish” means lacking spiritual understanding, unable to perceive what is right before God. “Disobedient” describes resistance to God’s authority, which in turn shows itself in resistance to human authority. “Deceived” pictures being led astray by a false guide. “Serving divers lusts and pleasures” is the language of slavery: people who imagined themselves free were in bondage to a variety of cravings and gratifications. The inward disorder then breaks out in relationships—“living in malice and envy,” ill will toward others and resentment of their good. The final pair, “hateful, and hating one another,” shows hostility becoming mutual and self-perpetuating.

Paul does not exaggerate for effect. He uses similar language of the Corinthians and Ephesians before conversion, and he knew from his own past as a persecutor how far a religious person can be from God. Remembering this condition guards against two dangers. It prevents contempt for unbelievers, since grace alone made the difference. It also forbids any return to the old life, for that life was slavery from which God has set believers free.

The dark background prepares for the turning point of verse 4. The worse the condition, the more striking the kindness that came to meet it.

wordNotes.term: δουλεύοντες ἐπιθυμίαις καὶ ἡδοναῖς ποικίλαις (douleuontes epithymiais kai hēdonais poikilais) — serving divers lusts and pleasures
wordNotes.explanation: The participle means “being slaves to.” Desires and pleasures are pictured as masters, and “divers” stresses their variety. Greek moralists lamented the tyranny of passion, but Paul sees it as part of a bondage from which only God’s grace delivers.

wordNotes.term: στυγητοί (stygētoi) — hateful
wordNotes.explanation: Found only here in the New Testament, the word can mean “hated” or “detestable.” In this list it describes people whose conduct makes them odious, and it leads naturally to the closing phrase about hating one another. Hostility given and received becomes a closed circle.

verses.bibleText: But after that the kindness and love of God our Saviour toward man appeared,

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“But after that” marks the decisive turn. Into the bleak condition of verse 3 came something from God’s side. Paul names it “the kindness and love of God our Saviour toward man.” Kindness speaks of God’s generous goodness; the second term, often rendered “love toward man,” is the Greek word from which “philanthropy” comes. In the wider culture it described the benevolence of a gracious ruler toward subjects or of a benefactor who ransomed captives. Cretans accustomed to hearing earthly rulers praised for such virtues are told where true benevolence comes from. Inscriptions across the Greek world honored emperors and governors as saviors and benefactors. The gospel claims those titles for God, whose generosity reached people who had nothing to offer him in return.

This kindness “appeared.” The verb is the same one used in 2:11 of the grace that brings salvation, and it echoes the noun used in 2:13 for Christ’s glorious appearing. Titus thus speaks of grace appearing, glory to appear, and kindness having appeared. The kindness appeared historically in the coming, life, death, and resurrection of Jesus, and it appeared personally to the Cretans when the gospel reached them and changed them.

In this verse “God our Saviour” refers to the Father, while verse 6 gives the same title to Jesus Christ. The letter moves freely between the two because the Father and the Son share one saving purpose. The Father is the source of the kindness, the Son its embodiment, and, as verse 5 will show, the Spirit its active agent. Believers who have received such kindness can hardly withhold kindness from others; the logic of verses 1–2 rests here.

wordNotes.term: ἡ χρηστότης καὶ ἡ φιλανθρωπία (hē chrēstotēs kai hē philanthrōpia) — the kindness and love toward man
wordNotes.explanation: Chrēstotēs is God’s generous goodness, which Paul says leads to repentance. Philanthrōpia was a familiar civic virtue praised in rulers and benefactors; Luke uses it of the islanders’ kindness to Paul after the shipwreck. Joined here, the two words present God as the true benefactor of humanity.

wordNotes.term: ἐπεφάνη (epephanē) — appeared
wordNotes.explanation: The verb means to shine forth or become visible. Paul uses it of God’s grace appearing in Christ’s first coming, and the related noun describes his future visible return. Salvation in Titus is framed between these two appearings.

verses.bibleText: Not by works of righteousness which we have done, but according to his mercy he saved us, by the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The main verb of the long sentence running from verse 4 to verse 7 is “he saved us.” Everything else explains the basis, the means, and the goal of that salvation. Paul first clears away any human claim: “Not by works of righteousness which we have done.” The phrase is emphatic in Greek, stressing deeds that we ourselves performed. Whether pre-Christian moral effort or religious observance, nothing we did supplied the ground on which God acted. The verse 3 portrait has already shown why. People enslaved to desire and living in malice have no righteous record to present.

The positive basis is God’s own “mercy.” Grace highlights favor toward the undeserving; mercy highlights compassion toward the wretched. God looked on human misery and acted out of pity. Salvation rests on his character, which is why it can be sure. A believer troubled by the memory of past sins does not have to search his record for reasons God might accept him. The reason lies in God’s compassion, and that does not shift with the believer’s moods.

The means are described as “the washing of regeneration, and renewing of the Holy Ghost.” Regeneration means new birth or a new beginning, and the washing is the cleansing that accompanies it. The background is the promise of Ezekiel 36, where God pledges to sprinkle clean water on his people, cleanse them from idols, give them a new heart, and put his Spirit within them so that they walk in his statutes. Jesus spoke to Nicodemus of being born of water and of the Spirit in the same prophetic frame. Cleansing from the past and renewal for a new life are God’s work within.

The language of washing would naturally remind early believers of baptism, which was the public sign of entering the new life. Baptism, however, is the sign and confession of what God does, and the water does not by itself regenerate anyone. Paul is describing the Spirit’s cleansing of the heart, received through repentance and faith; the rite has no mechanical or automatic power to save. Baptism rightly follows that inner change and testifies to it before the church and the world.

“Renewing” points to the new creation that the Spirit brings into being. It begins at conversion and continues as the mind is transformed day by day. The same Spirit who gives the new start goes on making believers new, so that the life once marked by verse 3 increasingly reflects the character of God.

wordNotes.term: λουτροῦ παλιγγενεσίας (loutrou palingenesias) — the washing of regeneration
wordNotes.explanation: Loutron denotes the act of washing; its only other New Testament use is Ephesians 5:26, where Christ cleanses the church by the washing of water with the word. Palingenesia, “new beginning” or “rebirth,” appears elsewhere only of the renewal of all things in the coming kingdom. Here it is applied to the individual: God gives a new beginning now that anticipates the renewed creation. The washing is inward cleansing from sin, of which baptism is the visible sign.

wordNotes.term: ἀνακαινώσεως πνεύματος ἁγίου (anakainōseōs pneumatos hagiou) — renewing of the Holy Ghost
wordNotes.explanation: Anakainōsis means a making new. The genitive identifies the Holy Spirit as the one who accomplishes it. Paul uses the same noun for the ongoing renewal of the mind, showing that the new birth opens a lifelong process of transformation.

verses.bibleText: Which he shed on us abundantly through Jesus Christ our Saviour;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“Which he shed on us” refers to the Holy Spirit just named. God the Father is the giver, and the verb “shed” means poured out, the word used in Joel’s prophecy and in Peter’s sermon at Pentecost. Paul thus links the personal experience of the Cretan believers with that historic outpouring. What happened in Jerusalem was not a single event for a few; it opened an age in which the Spirit is given to every believer.

“Abundantly” means richly or generously. God does not ration the Spirit. The same adverb describes the word of Christ dwelling richly in believers and God giving richly all things to enjoy. A church troubled by false teachers and weak habits did not need a new technique; it needed to rely on the abundant supply God had already provided.

The outpouring came “through Jesus Christ our Saviour.” The exalted Christ, having received the promise of the Spirit from the Father, poured it out on his people. In verses 4–6 the Father who saves, the Spirit who renews, and the Son through whom the Spirit is given work together in one act of salvation.

The repeated title “Saviour” ties the Son to the Father of verse 4. The Spirit is never detached from Christ; he comes as the gift of the risen Lord and makes Christ’s saving work effective in the believer’s life. Every renewal the Cretans experienced was a fruit of what Jesus had accomplished for them.

wordNotes.term: ἐξέχεεν ἐφ᾽ ἡμᾶς πλουσίως (execheen eph’ hēmas plousiōs) — he shed on us abundantly
wordNotes.explanation: Ekcheō is used of liquid poured out freely and is the verb of Joel’s promise in the Greek Old Testament. The aorist looks back to a completed outpouring, while plousiōs, “richly,” stresses the generosity of the gift.

verses.bibleText: That being justified by his grace, we should be made heirs according to the hope of eternal life.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
This verse states the purpose of God’s saving work. “That being justified by his grace” uses the language Paul employs in Romans and Galatians: to be justified is to be declared righteous by God, acquitted and accepted in his sight. The participle points to something already accomplished. The basis is “his grace,” with an emphatic pronoun pointing back to God our Saviour. As in verse 5, the source is entirely in God.

Justification and renewal belong together without being confused. Verse 5 describes the Spirit’s inner work; verse 7 describes the believer’s standing before God. No one is declared righteous who is left unchanged, and no one is changed apart from God’s pardoning grace. The order of the sentence keeps the emphasis on God, who both forgives and transforms.

The goal is that “we should be made heirs.” An heir has a secure title to an inheritance that is not yet fully received. Believers are sons and daughters of God who share Christ’s inheritance, and that relationship continues as long as they abide in the Father’s family. The inheritance is defined as “eternal life,” and it is held “according to the hope.” Eternal life is God’s gift, begun now in fellowship with him and given in its fullness when Christ appears and the dead in Christ are raised, when mortality puts on immortality. The letter opened with the “hope of eternal life, which God, that cannot lie, promised” (1:2), and the body of the letter now closes on the same note.

The heirs therefore live between possession and fulfillment. They are already justified and renewed, yet they look for the blessed hope (2:13). That hope, resting on God’s promise rather than on present circumstances, steadies them amid hostility and gives them reason to deal kindly with those who have not yet received the same mercy.

wordNotes.term: δικαιωθέντες τῇ ἐκείνου χάριτι (dikaiōthentes tē ekeinou chariti) — being justified by his grace
wordNotes.explanation: The aorist passive participle describes an act God has performed on the believer’s behalf. Ekeinou, “of that one,” points emphatically to God. The phrase echoes Romans 3:24, where justification is freely given through the redemption in Christ.

wordNotes.term: κληρονόμοι … κατ᾽ ἐλπίδα ζωῆς αἰωνίου (klēronomoi … kat’ elpida zōēs aiōniou) — heirs according to the hope of eternal life
wordNotes.explanation: An heir has the right to an inheritance not yet taken in hand. The phrase “according to hope” shows that the inheritance is assured but future. Eternal life is the content of that hope, granted in full at the resurrection when Christ returns.

verses.bibleText: This is a faithful saying, and these things I will that thou affirm constantly, that they which have believed in God might be careful to maintain good works. These things are good and profitable unto men.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“This is a faithful saying” is a formula found five times in the Pastoral Letters, marking a statement as reliable and worthy of full acceptance. Here it points back to the summary of salvation in verses 4–7, which may have been a confession used in the churches, perhaps at baptism. Paul sets his apostolic seal on it.

“These things I will that thou affirm constantly” calls Titus to speak with settled confidence. The verb is the same one Paul used of false teachers who confidently affirmed what they did not understand. Titus is to be equally insistent, but about truth that saves. The repeated rehearsal of God’s mercy is not stale for believers. Each return to the gospel story renews gratitude and courage.

The purpose of such teaching is “that they which have believed in God might be careful to maintain good works.” The perfect participle describes those who came to faith and continue in it. “Careful” means to give thought, to set the mind on something. “Maintain” can mean to take the lead in, to make it one’s business. Believers who have received salvation apart from works are to be foremost in doing good. Grace never makes good works optional; it is the source from which they flow, just as 2:14 described a people zealous of good works.

“These things are good and profitable unto men.” The sound teaching and the good works it produces are excellent in themselves and beneficial to people, including the unbelieving neighbors in view since verse 1. The contrast is sharpened in the next verse, where the false teachers’ concerns are dismissed as unprofitable and vain. The test of any teaching is whether it leaves people better and more useful.

wordNotes.term: πιστὸς ὁ λόγος (pistos ho logos) — this is a faithful saying
wordNotes.explanation: The formula commends a compact statement of truth as trustworthy. In each occurrence it relates to salvation or to the life it produces. Here it refers back to the preceding confession about God’s mercy, regeneration, justification, and hope.

wordNotes.term: καλῶν ἔργων προΐστασθαι (kalōn ergōn proistasthai) — to maintain good works
wordNotes.explanation: The verb literally means to stand before or to lead, and in the Pastoral Letters it often describes leadership. With good works it suggests making them a priority and leading the way in them. A few translations suggest “honest occupations,” yet the letter consistently uses the phrase of good deeds, which fits better.

verses.bibleText: But avoid foolish questions, and genealogies, and contentions, and strivings about the law; for they are unprofitable and vain.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Over against the profitable teaching of verse 8 Paul sets four things Titus must avoid. “Foolish questions” are speculative disputes that produce argument without wisdom. “Genealogies” were elaborate theories built on Old Testament family lists and legends, apparently treated as keys to hidden spiritual knowledge; Paul named the same problem in Ephesus. “Contentions” are the rivalries such debates provoke. “Strivings about the law” are quarrels over the Mosaic law, likely concerning the purity rules, traditions, and fables that Jewish-leaning teachers on Crete were pressing (1:10, 14).

Paul’s objection is not to the law itself, which he elsewhere calls good when used lawfully, nor to careful study of Scripture. The law that reveals God’s will remains holy, just, and good. The problem lay in turning Scripture into a field for clever speculation and party conflict, so that people argued about the law while ignoring its call to love God and neighbor. Such discussions changed no one’s character.

The verb “avoid” means to turn aside, to step around something so as to go the other way. Titus was not to give these debates a platform. The reason is plain: “they are unprofitable and vain,” the opposite of the good and profitable things just commended. A church can lose its energy and its witness to arguments that never lead anyone to repentance or holy living. The pastor’s task is to steer the congregation back to the gospel of verses 4–7 and the good works it produces.

wordNotes.term: μάχας νομικάς (machas nomikas) — strivings about the law
wordNotes.explanation: Machē means a fight or quarrel; nomikos means concerning the law. The phrase describes disputes centered on the Mosaic law as the false teachers used it, with its traditions and speculations. Paul’s concern is the quarrelsome misuse, since he affirms that the law is good when used rightly.

wordNotes.term: περιΐστασο (periistaso) — avoid
wordNotes.explanation: The middle imperative means to go around so as to avoid, to shun. Paul gives Timothy the same counsel about profane and empty chatter. The present tense suggests a settled practice of refusing such debates.

verses.bibleText: A man that is an heretick after the first and second admonition reject;

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Some in Crete would not simply indulge in the disputes of verse 9; they would make them a cause and gather followers around them. Paul calls such a person “an heretick.” The Greek word comes from a root meaning choice, and in this period it described someone who chooses a party and so creates division. The later technical sense of one who holds condemned doctrine is not yet fully present, though the person’s choice is set against the apostolic teaching. A modern rendering might be “a factious person.”

The procedure is patient. Titus is to give “the first and second admonition.” Admonition combines instruction with warning; it aims to change the will, not merely to win an argument. Each conversation should present clearly from Scripture why the views and conduct are wrong, giving the person a real opportunity to turn. Such a process recalls Jesus’ instruction to go first privately and then with witnesses before taking the matter to the church. The standard is God’s word, not the leader’s personal preferences.

Only after two warnings have been refused does Paul say “reject.” The verb means to refuse, decline, or have nothing more to do with. In this context it amounts to removing the divisive person from the fellowship and influence of the church. The step protects the flock from ongoing harm, and it also leaves the person to face the seriousness of his choice. Church discipline in Scripture is never casual or vindictive; it is a last resort taken for the health of the body and in hope of eventual repentance.

wordNotes.term: αἱρετικὸν ἄνθρωπον (hairetikon anthrōpon) — a man that is an heretick
wordNotes.explanation: Hairetikos, used only here in the New Testament, is related to hairesis, which can describe a party or sect. It denotes one who promotes faction by choosing his own way against the apostolic message. Paul lists such factions among the works of the flesh.

wordNotes.term: νουθεσίαν (nouthesian) — admonition
wordNotes.explanation: This noun, used only by Paul in the New Testament, combines teaching with warning. It appears in the instruction of children and in the lessons drawn from Israel’s history. Its purpose is correction that leads to change.

verses.bibleText: Knowing that he that is such is subverted, and sinneth, being condemned of himself.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul explains why Titus may take the step of rejection with a clear conscience. “Knowing” indicates that the decision rests on evidence gathered through the admonitions, not on suspicion. The person who refuses repeated correction has shown what he is.

“Subverted” translates a perfect-tense verb meaning turned inside out or twisted, a settled condition of having turned away from the truth. “Sinneth” is in the present tense: he continues in his course even after being warned. Finally he is “condemned of himself.” His own choices and his refusal of correction pronounce the verdict; the church merely recognizes it. Conscience, which he has overridden, testifies against him.

Paul has already described the false teachers as those whose “mind and conscience is defiled” (1:15). The factious person of verse 10 has followed the same path, and the warnings he refused were the means by which God was calling him back.

The verse relieves leaders of the burden of trying endlessly to win a person who has determined not to be won. It also warns every believer that persistent refusal of loving correction can harden the heart until it no longer hears.

wordNotes.term: ἐξέστραπται (exestraptai) — is subverted
wordNotes.explanation: The verb, found only here in the New Testament, means to turn out or twist. The perfect tense describes a settled condition. The Greek Old Testament uses it of a perverse and crooked generation.

wordNotes.term: αὐτοκατάκριτος (autokatakritos) — condemned of himself
wordNotes.explanation: This compound, another New Testament hapax, means self-condemned. The person’s own persistence in sin after warning supplies the ground of judgment, much as Paul describes those who condemn themselves in the things they approve.

verses.bibleText: When I shall send Artemas unto thee, or Tychicus, be diligent to come unto me to Nicopolis: for I have determined there to winter.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
The letter now turns to plans. Paul intends to send either Artemas or Tychicus to Crete, and when one arrives Titus is to hurry to join Paul at Nicopolis. Artemas is mentioned nowhere else. Tychicus was a trusted colleague from the province of Asia who traveled with Paul to Jerusalem and carried his letters to Ephesus and Colossae. Paul has not yet decided which man to send, yet he will not leave the young churches without a leader while Titus is away.

Nicopolis, “city of victory,” was a name given to several towns, but the most likely is the city in Epirus on the western coast of Greece, founded by Augustus to commemorate the battle of Actium. It would be a strategic base for work along the Adriatic. Second Timothy later notes that Titus went to Dalmatia, just to the north, which fits this plan.

“I have determined there to winter” reflects the realities of ancient travel. Sailing on the Mediterranean was dangerous and largely suspended in the winter months, so missionaries planned their movements accordingly. Paul’s determination to spend those months with a coworker shows how he valued fellowship and kept planning for further gospel work. Ministry in Scripture is shared labor; even the apostle depended on companions and arranged for the care of the churches he could not personally visit.

wordNotes.term: σπούδασον ἐλθεῖν (spoudason elthein) — be diligent to come
wordNotes.explanation: The aorist imperative of spoudazō means to make haste or make every effort. Paul uses the same urgent request when asking Timothy to come to him before winter.

verses.bibleText: Bring Zenas the lawyer and Apollos on their journey diligently, that nothing be wanting unto them.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Two more travelers are commended to Titus. Zenas is described by his profession as “the lawyer.” The word could refer to an expert in Jewish law, as in the Gospels, but his Greek name makes training in Roman law at least as likely. Nothing more is known of him. Apollos is the eloquent Alexandrian, mighty in the Scriptures, whom Priscilla and Aquila instructed and who watered what Paul had planted in Corinth. The two may have carried this letter to Crete on their way to another field.

“Bring … on their journey diligently” translates a verb that meant sending travelers onward with provisions, funds, and arrangements for the next stage. Early Christian mission relied on this kind of practical support. Titus is to see that “nothing be wanting unto them.” Hospitality to traveling workers was a concrete form of partnership in the gospel, a way for local believers to share in labor they could not do in person.

The mention of Apollos also says something about Paul. Some at Corinth had once set Apollos against Paul as the leader of a rival party, yet Paul shows no trace of competition. He asks Titus to equip Apollos generously, because both men served the same Lord and labored in the same field.

wordNotes.term: πρόπεμψον (propempson) — bring on their journey
wordNotes.explanation: Propempō means to escort or send someone forward, usually supplying what is needed for travel. Paul hoped the Roman believers would send him on toward Spain in this way, and John commends those who send missionaries forward worthily of God.

verses.bibleText: And let our's also learn to maintain good works for necessary uses, that they be not unfruitful.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
“And let our’s also learn” widens the instruction from Titus to the Cretan believers as a whole. Supplying Zenas and Apollos was not to be a task for one leader alone. The congregations were to share it, and in doing so to learn a habit. Good works have to be learned; they become part of a community’s character through practice.

The phrase “to maintain good works” repeats the wording of verse 8, so Paul returns to his main concern just before the greetings. Now he adds the purpose: “for necessary uses.” The expression points to urgent needs, the practical wants of travelers, the poor, and the struggling. Good works are not vague religious sentiment; they meet real requirements in real lives. Some read the phrase as honest work that supplies one’s own needs and those of others, a sense close to Paul’s counsel elsewhere that believers labor with their hands so they can give. Either reading keeps good works practical.

“That they be not unfruitful” brings the contrast with the false teachers into focus once more. Those teachers professed to know God but were “unto every good work reprobate” (1:16), and their debates were unprofitable and vain. A church that learns to meet needs bears fruit that commends the gospel. Jesus taught that a tree is known by its fruit, and Paul ends his instructions by asking the Cretans to be a fruitful tree.

wordNotes.term: εἰς τὰς ἀναγκαίας χρείας (eis tas anankaias chreias) — for necessary uses
wordNotes.explanation: Chreia means a need or lack, and anankaios means pressing or indispensable. The phrase describes urgent necessities. Paul thanked the Philippians for supplying his need, and the early church distributed to each as any had need.

wordNotes.term: ἄκαρποι (akarpoi) — unfruitful
wordNotes.explanation: The word describes a plant that yields no fruit. In the New Testament it is applied to the word choked by worldly cares and to a faith lacking virtue and knowledge. Paul wants the Cretan believers to be fruitful in practical good.

verses.bibleText: All that are with me salute thee. Greet them that love us in the faith. Grace be with you all. Amen.

commentary.detailedExplanation:
Paul closes with greetings in both directions. “All that are with me” refers to his traveling companions, who are not named. Titus in turn is to “greet them that love us in the faith.” The phrase defines the circle of fellowship by shared trust in Christ and mutual affection, perhaps with a quiet distinction from the false teachers who had set themselves against Paul.

Even in a short greeting the letter’s concerns appear. Love and faith belong together, and the fellowship of believers is held by both. Those who love the apostle in the faith also receive his teaching, while those who resist it have placed themselves outside that circle of warm communion.

The benediction, “Grace be with you all,” uses a plural pronoun. Although the letter was addressed to Titus, Paul expected it to be read to the congregations. The letter that began with grace from God the Father and the Lord Jesus Christ (1:4) ends by commending the whole church to that same grace, which teaches godly living (2:11–12) and justifies the believer (3:7).

wordNotes.term: τοὺς φιλοῦντας ἡμᾶς ἐν πίστει (tous philountas hēmas en pistei) — them that love us in the faith
wordNotes.explanation: Phileō expresses warm personal affection. The phrase “in faith” may mean within the Christian faith or faithfully. Either way, the greeting identifies those bound to Paul by shared trust in Christ.

teachingNotes.openingQuestion: How should the memory of what God rescued us from shape the way we treat people who do not yet share our faith?
teachingNotes.mainPoint: God saved us by his own mercy through the Spirit’s new birth, and that undeserved kindness makes believers gentle neighbors, diligent in good works, and unwilling to waste the church’s life on profitless quarrels.
discussionQuestions: Why does Paul place a description of our former life immediately after a call to gentleness toward all people?
How do the washing of regeneration and the renewing of the Holy Spirit describe both the beginning and the continuation of new life?
What does it mean to take the lead in good works, and how does verse 14 make that concrete?
How can a church distinguish healthy study of Scripture from the foolish questions Paul tells Titus to avoid?
What does the two-step admonition of verse 10 teach about patience and firmness in church discipline?
commonMisunderstandings: Submission to rulers is not unlimited; readiness for every good work leaves the believer free to obey God rather than men when the two conflict.
The washing of regeneration is the Spirit’s inner cleansing, which baptism signifies; the rite has no saving power in itself.
Rejecting a factious person follows patient admonition and aims at protecting the church, not at punishing honest questions.
Being saved apart from works does not make good works optional; it makes them the expected fruit of mercy received.
teachingNotes.emphasis: Keep the doctrine and the duty together: the kindness of God our Saviour is both the reason believers can be gentle with others and the power that produces their good works.
teachingNotes.closingAppeal: Remember who you were without Christ, receive again the mercy that washed and renewed you, and let that mercy make you a peacemaker and a helper of others this week.

evangelisticNotes.mainDoctrinalTheme: God saves sinners by his mercy alone, cleansing and renewing them through the Holy Spirit poured out through Jesus Christ, and makes them heirs of eternal life.
flow: Without God, human life drifts into folly, bondage to desire, and mutual hostility.
God’s kindness and love toward humanity appeared in Jesus Christ.
He saves by mercy, not by any righteous deeds we bring.
The Holy Spirit washes and renews the heart, and baptism publicly signifies that new birth.
The justified become heirs who wait in hope for eternal life at Christ’s appearing.
simpleIllustrations: A prisoner freed by a benefactor who paid his ransom does not boast of earning his release; he lives gratefully as one set free.
A garden plot cleared of weeds is only the beginning; it needs living seed and steady rain to become fruitful, just as cleansing is followed by the Spirit’s renewal.
evangelisticNotes.appealQuestion: Will you stop relying on what you have done and receive the mercy of God, asking his Spirit to wash and renew your life?
cautions: Do not present baptism as a ritual that saves apart from repentance, faith, and the Spirit’s work.
Do not describe the former life in a way that encourages contempt for those who are still outside Christ.
Do not imply that eternal life is already fully possessed; it is the hope of heirs who await the resurrection.

reflectionQuestions: Which person or authority do I find hardest to treat with gentleness, and how does God’s kindness to me change my response?
What part of my former life do I most need to remember with humility rather than pride?
Where am I still tempted to rest my standing with God on my own record instead of his mercy?
What practical need near me could I meet this week as an act of good works?
Am I drawn into arguments that generate heat but produce no godliness, and what would it look like to step away?
